title: Day Around the Bay: Posey Tube Reopens Early, After Much Traffic Mess
summary: Rainbow Grocery cleaned up from some flooding last week in time for Thanksgiving shopping; Marin County only saw minor flooding today; and the Posey Tube between Alameda and Oakland has reopened ahead of schedule.
content: Local: Flooding in the basement of Rainbow Grocery last week forced a two-day closure of the store, but they managed to clean up and reopen ahead of Thanksgiving — and implored regular customers to please come in and shop to make up for the missed days. [ Chronicle ] Marin County saw minor flooding today, but the amount of rain that fell — far less than was forecast — helped prevent any major flood catastrophes there. [ NBC Bay Area ] The closure of the Posey Tube between Alameda and Oakland — the tunnel that leads off the island, parallel to the inbound Webster Tube — ahead of this week's predicted storms set off a bunch of traffic impacts across the small island, and so it is reopening ahead of schedule. [ Chronicle ] National: A federal judge has shut down the Trump administration's effort to punish ABC and its affiliate stations for political reasons, siding with parent company Disney in the First Amendment case. KGO/ABC 7 in the Bay Are was among the affiliates being targeted for license non-renewal under the Trump-appointee-led FCC. [ CNN ] In case you had not already heard, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in its 100-year history. Due to extreme weather, it will be on Saturday, instead. [ CBS News ] Andy Taylor, guitarist for the band Duran Duran, has died at age 65. [ New York Times ] Video: National treasure Ina Garten has a new podcast (on video) called Happy Hour, where she doesn't cook anything, but she talks about food and entertaining and other things with celebrities and other celebrity chefs, and she has a new episode talking about all things Thanksgiving with Seth Meyers, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jennifer Garner, and Bobby Flay. What time should Thanksgiving start? Seth says 3 pm, Ina says 6 pm.

title: SF’s Old Bay Bridge Steel Lives on Through Public Art Across California
summary: Hundreds of tons of steel from the old Bay Bridge have been repurposed into public art and functional installations across California, including benches overlooking the new bridge, sculptures on Treasure Island, and a miniature train station in Truckee.
content: Hundreds of tons of steel from the old Bay Bridge have been repurposed into public art and functional installations across California, including benches overlooking the new bridge, sculptures on Treasure Island, and a miniature train station in Truckee. After the eastern span was demolished in 2014, the Toll Bridge Program Oversight Committee established the Bay Bridge Steel Program in response to interest from local artists and creative organizations. The Oakland Museum of California administered the program, distributing approximately 450 tons of salvaged steel to artists, architects, and design firms for 14 projects intended to commemorate the bridge's history while remaining accessible to the public. The steel was provided free of charge, but recipients were responsible for transportation, storage, fabrication, and securing any necessary local approvals. Bayfront Park in Mission Bay; Kristine K/Yelp San Francisco-based landscape architecture firm Surfacedesign received the largest allocation, incorporating the steel into Bayfront Park, the new 5.5-acre waterfront park in Mission Bay. As SFist reported previously, repurposed beams serve as seating areas, while other pieces are incorporated into sculptural features, shade structures, and an observation deck overlooking the new Bay Bridge. According to SFGate , the location also has a connection to San Francisco's industrial history, as the waterfront site was once part of Bethlehem Steel. Landscape architect Michal Kapitulnik said the opportunity to select steel directly from the old span was a once-in-a-lifetime experience. “Connecting that narrative of the material and industrial heritage of Mission Bay to the construction of the Bay Bridge and then bringing that steel back to the site was really exciting for us,” Kapitulnik said, speaking to SFGate. via The Old Lumberyard In Joshua Tree, Oakland artist Mark Bulwinkle created an elaborate entrance gate for the Harrison House Music Arts and Ecology Center. In Truckee, Mountain Forge used eight tons of steel to build a miniature train station at Truckee River Regional Park, incorporating one of the bridge's original warning lights. Leftover steel is also being used for illuminated fire pits at downtown Truckee's Old Lumberyard. Tom Loughlin's Signal on Treasure Island; Tom Loughlin/Google Maps Treasure Island has two major installations. Tom Loughlin's Signal , a circular sculpture made from sections of massive bridge girders, has provided seating and bay views since 2019. Petaluma sculptor Sean Paul Lorentz received approximately 70 tons of steel and has used it to create several large-scale works, including sculptures displayed in California and Tennessee. Even the smallest pieces found a purpose. The Living New Deal received 20 rivets for its Building Bridges, Not Walls exhibition, highlighting the contributions of immigrant workers who helped build the Bay Bridge and Golden Gate Bridge. The Elsewhere Philatelic Society also received five rivets for interactive performances exploring the bridge's history. Per SFGate, only seven of the selected 14 projects have been completed so far, with others delayed by construction, funding, and difficulties finding suitable locations. Other remnants of the old span can be found at Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline and Gateway Park, where salvaged steel was used in an observation pier connecting the East Bay to Treasure Island. Yerba Buena Island's Bimla Rhinehart Vista Point also has a picnic table, bike racks, and other accents made from the material. There's also still more steel available. Karin Betts of the Metropolitan Transportation Commission told SFGate in 2024 that officials had yet to decide whether to distribute it through another artist program or save it for future projects at Shoreline Park. Related: SF’s Newest Park Just Opened Right Next to Chase Center, Featuring Steel Beams From the Old Bay Bridge
